FROM: Chairman Thomas J. Gleeson 2—
DATE: March 11, 2026

RE: March 12, 2026, Open Meeting — Item No. 42

Project No. 58481 — Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection
Standards Under § PURA 37.0561

Before the Commission for consideration is the proposal for publication implementing
Public Utility Regulatory Act § 37.0561 and establishing Large Load Interconnection Standards
for the ERCOT region. This rulemaking takes a significant step toward modernizing and
standardizing the large-load interconnection process. I appreciate Staffs and ERCOT’s efforts to
develop this draft rule; however, I believe we should adjust two of the draft rule’s provisions to
materially improve how we balance the state’s economic development interests with safeguarding
the reliability of the ERCOT transmission system:

1. Adjusting the proposed $100,000 per MW financial requirements, and

2. Expanding the definition of “site control” to include purchase and sale agreements.

Adjustment to Dollar-per-MW Financial Requirements

The draft rule would require large load customers to post financial security and pay
interconnection fees calculated at $100,000 per MW. I understand that Staff proposed this
threshold to put an end to the frustrating transmission planning restudy cycle caused by a ceaseless
stream of speculative large load projects claiming to desire immediate interconnection to the
ERCOT system. While I strongly support the objective, I am concerned that the dollar amount
proposed by Staff may unintentionally deter otherwise viable development.

The $100,000 per MW threshold may unintentionally create a barrier to market entry for
all but the largest hyperscalers in the world, even if these smaller companies have viable, tangible
projects under development. Moreover, the proposal to require payment of the financial security
at the intermediate agreement stage — even before ERCOT conducts its interconnection study —
could obligate customers to secure funding far in excess of the actual interconnection costs,
creating unnecessary financial issues early in project development. To strike a more appropriate
balance between reliability, cost protection, and market participation, I recommend reducing the
requirement to $50,000 per MW.

 This amount remains meaningful, sufficiently discourages speculative applications, and
still advances the Commission’s overarching goal of promoting transparency and predictability in
the interconnection process.

Expansion of Acceptable Demonstrations of Site Control

PURA § 37.0561(g) authorizes site control to be demonstrated through “ownership, lease,
or another legal interest acceptable to the commission.” The draft rule currently recognizes only
executed leases and deeds. While these remain appropriate, the rule should also allow a project
developer to execute an option to lease or buy land as acceptable evidence of site control in the
early phases of the large load interconnection process.

Options to lease or buy are common tools used by developers to secure site control for a
limited time period while minimizing financial risks should the proposed project fall through.
Here, we should allow a large load to provide an executed option to lease or buy the site at the
intermediate agreement phase. Such an allowance would correctly align the rule with typical
business processes at this early phase of the interconnection process, a stage at which a viable large
load project is still learning about the electrical facilities that would be required to energize the
load.

At the interconnection agreement phase—once the load learns what transmission projects
would be necessary to interconnect it to the system—it would be appropriate for the Commission
to require a higher standard of evidence. In addition to the types of agreements proposed in
subsection (f)(1), expressly adding Purchase and Sales Agreements (PSAs), would provide
tangible benefits to both the grid and the businesses it serves. PSAs are widely used in commercial
development and large-scale infrastructure projects. They typically include binding commitments,
detailed property descriptions, and enforceable closing conditions, which provide meaningful
assurance that the applicant has secured the right to the land necessary for the project. In many
cases, developers cannot or should not close on property until certain regulatory or financial
milestones are satisfied. Recognizing PSAs as an approved basis for site control at the
interconnection agreement phase aligns Commission rules with established market practice and
avoids imposing unnecessary burdens on customers.

I appreciate Staff's efforts on this important rulemaking and look forward to discussing
these recommendations at the open meeting.
